This section is front matter plus the opening of Chapter 1, "Standard Equipment" (file pages 1–5 are blurbs, author biography, contents, and Preface; the substantive text begins on file page 6). The Preface states the book's two organizing ideas: the computational theory of mind and natural selection of replicators, with the mind described as a system of organs of computation shaped to solve ancestral problems (file page 4). Pinker explicitly warns that we do not yet understand the mind well, that every idea may prove wrong, and that he presents a selective synthesis rather than comprehensive reviews of all debates (file pages 4–5). Language is deliberately excluded, covered in his earlier book (file page 4).

The chapter's subject is the "robot challenge": the engineering difficulty of ordinary seeing, walking, grasping, thinking, and planning, which Pinker treats as both a design specification for robots and the subject matter of psychology (file pages 6–7). He rejects single-cause explanations—brain size, culture, language, learning, complexity, self-organization, neural-network dynamics—arguing instead that the mind is packed with specialized systems, each solving its own problem (file pages 6–7). He stresses that mental faculties are opaque to introspection, which breeds the illusion of a single animating essence (file page 6).

Perception receives the most detailed treatment. Pinker shows that a robot's visual input is a grid of brightness values, not a picture, and that recovering objects from these numbers is "humblingly difficult" (file pages 7–8). Edge detection fails because a brightness boundary could reflect occlusion, paint, shadow, contact, corners, or translucent overlays; the Sinha and Adelson figure demonstrates that identical gray patches arise from different physical arrangements (file page 8). He describes a chicken-and-egg problem: identifying objects requires knowing what each patch is, and knowing what a patch is requires knowing the object (file page 8). Lightness perception must discount illumination, since more light bounces off outdoor coal than indoor snow; the visual system nonetheless sees coal as black and snow as white, matching the world rather than the retinal image (file page 8–9). Television screens exploit this: perceived black is actually the pale phosphor gray (file page 9). Depth is lost in projection and must be reconstructed; the same retinal square or trapezoid can come from objects at very different distances, illustrated by afterimages that scale with the surface viewed (file page 9).

Pinker then considers object recognition. A template matching each shape fails in both directions: it falsely matches similar letters and misses the target when shifted, tilted, scaled, or stylized (file pages 9–10). This is the clearest statement of a generalization problem in the section: a rule must cover permitted variations without memorizing every instance or over-extending.

Engineering implications, kept separate: the section supports building perception as inference over ambiguous signals, with representations tied to world properties (material, depth, illumination) rather than raw pixels, and with recognition schemes tolerant of transformation. It does not yet address compositionality, semantics, memory, time, causation, goals, reasoning, analogy, creativity, emotion, or social cognition; those appear in later chapters per the contents (file page 3). Nothing here establishes universal learning laws, and the text is not about non-neural machines specifically. The pixel array and figure-dependent demonstrations (file pages 7–9) are visually grounded and partly garbled in plain text; their exact appearance is uncertain.
